main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English Language skills
specific_competence_name: Develop listening and speaking skills
learning_activity_name: Write dictated words
sla_name: Dictation of names of animals
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly spells and writes at least four dictated animal names such as lion, elephant, giraffe and zebra without teacher assistance.
sla_teaching_aids: Word cards with animal names|Chalkboard|Exercise books|Pictures of animals
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Dictation involves listening carefully to words read aloud by the teacher and writing them down correctly, spelling each word as it is heard. Names of animals are used as the first set of dictation words.
sla_notes_details: The teacher reads each word clearly, repeats it if necessary, and pupils write it in their exercise books, paying attention to correct spelling and letter formation before the teacher marks the work.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example dictation list: lion, elephant, giraffe, buffalo, zebra, antelope, monkey — the very animals reported by pupils after their visit to the Serengeti National Park.
sla_notes_daily_life: Learning to write animal names correctly helps a pupil write about animals they see at home, on television, or during a visit to a zoo or national park.
sla_exercise: Listen and write: lion::lion||Listen and write: elephant::elephant||Listen and write: giraffe::giraffe||Listen and write: zebra::zebra

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English Language skills
specific_competence_name: Develop listening and speaking skills
learning_activity_name: Write dictated words
sla_name: Dictation of names of birds and insects
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly spells and writes at least four dictated names of birds or insects such as eagle, flamingo, bee and butterfly.
sla_teaching_aids: Word cards with bird and insect names|Chalkboard|Exercise books|Pictures of birds and insects
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Dictation of bird and insect names builds vocabulary and spelling skill using words pupils have already met, such as those seen during the class visit to the Serengeti National Park.
sla_notes_details: The teacher reads each word at normal speed and again slowly, and pupils listen and write the word, then check their spelling against the word card shown by the teacher.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example dictation list: eagle, ostrich, flamingo, crow, woodpecker, bee, wasp, grasshopper, ant, tsetse fly, butterfly.
sla_notes_daily_life: Pupils can use these words to write short notes about birds and insects they observe in their school compound or home garden.
sla_exercise: Listen and write: eagle::eagle||Listen and write: flamingo::flamingo||Listen and write: butterfly::butterfly||Listen and write: grasshopper::grasshopper

sla_name: Dictation of names of common objects

sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Dictated words may also be names of common objects used at home and school, such as knife, table, telephone, hammer, key, torch, spoon, umbrella and pot, the same objects used when describing uses of things.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example dictation list: knife, table, telephone, hammer, key, torch, spoon, umbrella, pot.
sla_notes_daily_life: Writing the correct names of household objects helps a pupil make a simple shopping list or write about tools used at home.
sla_exercise: Listen and write: umbrella::umbrella||Listen and write: telephone::telephone||Listen and write: hammer::hammer||Listen and write: spoon::spoon

sla_name: Writing dictated simple sentences
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly writes at least two dictated simple sentences with correct spelling, capital letters and full stops.
sla_teaching_aids: Chalkboard|Exercise books|Sentence cards
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: After mastering single words, pupils listen to short sentences read aloud by the teacher and write them correctly, including capital letters at the start and a full stop at the end.
sla_notes_details: The teacher reads a sentence once at normal speed, then slowly, and pupils write it; afterwards the teacher writes the sentence on the chalkboard so pupils can check and correct their own work.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example dictated sentences: 'The pen is used for writing.' and 'The ball is under the chair.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Writing dictated sentences accurately prepares a pupil to note down instructions or messages given by parents or teachers.
sla_exercise: Listen and write: The pen is used for writing.::The pen is used for writing.||Listen and write: The ball is under the chair.::The ball is under the chair.||Listen and write: The knife is used for cutting.::The knife is used for cutting.

sla_name: Naming animals, insects and objects orally
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly names at least five pictures of animals, insects or objects shown by the teacher, using complete English words.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of animals|Pictures of insects|Pictures of objects|Flashcards
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Naming things orally means looking at a picture and saying its correct English name aloud, which builds vocabulary for animals, insects and everyday objects.
sla_notes_details: The teacher shows pictures of animals, then insects, then objects one group at a time, and pupils take turns naming each picture correctly before moving to the next group.
sla_notes_illustrations: Pupils look at pictures of animals, insects and objects and name each one, for example lion, elephant, ant, butterfly, knife and umbrella.
sla_notes_daily_life: Naming things orally helps a pupil communicate clearly when pointing out animals, insects or objects to family members or friends.
sla_exercise: What is this animal called?::It is a lion.||What is this insect called?::It is a butterfly.||What is this object called?::It is an umbrella.

specific_competence_name: Develop listening and speaking skills

sla_name: Describing actions and uses of common objects orally
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil orally describes an action shown in a picture and correctly states the use of a given common object using the structure 'It is used for...'.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of people performing actions|Pictures of objects: pen, knife, hammer, telephone|Real objects
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Describing actions means saying what a person in a picture is doing. Describing uses means explaining what an object is used for, following the structure: 'What is the [object] used for? The [object] is used for [action].'
sla_notes_details: The teacher first shows pictures of people doing different actions for pupils to describe, then shows objects such as a knife, table, telephone, hammer, key, torch, spoon, umbrella and pot for pupils to describe their uses using the example: 'What is the pen used for? The pen is used for writing.'
sla_notes_illustrations: Example: What is the pen used for? The pen is used for writing. Other objects practised: knife, table, telephone, hammer, key, torch, spoon, umbrella, pot.
sla_notes_daily_life: Describing what objects are used for helps a pupil explain to a younger sibling how to use tools safely at home.
sla_exercise: What is the pen used for?::The pen is used for writing.||What is the knife used for?::The knife is used for cutting.||What is the umbrella used for?::The umbrella is used for protecting from rain or sun.||What is the telephone used for?::The telephone is used for communicating.

sla_name: Describing locations of objects using on, in and under
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly describes the location of an object shown in a picture using the prepositions on, in or under.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures showing objects in different locations|Real classroom objects|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Describing locations means telling where an object is placed, using the prepositions on, in or under, following the structure: 'Where is the [object]? The [object] is [preposition] the [place].'
sla_notes_details: The teacher shows pictures of objects placed on, in or under other things and pupils practise asking and answering location questions in pairs, following the book's example.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example: Where is the ball? The ball is under the chair.
sla_notes_daily_life: Describing where things are located helps a pupil give clear directions when someone asks where an item is kept at home or in class.
sla_exercise: Where is the ball?::The ball is under the chair.||Where is the book?::The book is on the table.||Where is the pencil?::The pencil is in the bag.

sla_name: Listening to short stories and answering questions: Bahati's room and The proud rose
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil listens attentively to a short story and correctly answers at least four oral comprehension questions about its characters, places and events.
sla_teaching_aids: Story text: Bahati's room|Story text: The proud rose|Pictures related to the stories
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Listening to oral texts means paying close attention to a story read by the teacher and understanding it well enough to answer questions about the characters, places and events.
sla_notes_details: In 'Bahati's room', pupils listen and then help Bahati find her belongings by answering where each item is located. In 'The proud rose', pupils listen and answer questions about why the rose was proud and what the other plants told it.
sla_notes_illustrations: Bahati's room questions: Where is the school bag? Where are the shoes? Where is the yellow blouse? Where is the pencil? Where are the T-shirts? The proud rose questions: Why was the rose so proud of itself? Where did the rose and cactus grow? Why did the rose complain? What did other plants tell the rose?
sla_notes_daily_life: Listening carefully to a story and answering questions about it helps a pupil follow instructions and stories told by parents, elders or on the radio at home.
sla_exercise: Where is the school bag in Bahati's room?::The school bag is behind the door, where Bahati had left it.||Where are the shoes in Bahati's room?::The shoes are under the bed.||Why was the rose so proud of itself?::The rose was proud because it thought it was the most beautiful plant in the garden.||What did other plants tell the rose?::The other plants told the rose to stop being proud and to respect other plants like the cactus.

sla_name: Reading aloud and oral practice: A trip to the Serengeti National Park
sla_method: Reading aloud and question and answer
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil reads aloud a short passage fluently and correctly answers at least five oral comprehension questions about the Serengeti National Park story, then takes part in paired oral practice about national parks.
sla_teaching_aids: Text: A trip to the Serengeti National Park|Pictures of national parks and wild animals|Pictures of birds
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Reading aloud means pronouncing written text clearly so that others can hear and understand. After reading, pupils answer oral questions to check understanding, and later practise asking and answering questions in pairs about national parks.
sla_notes_details: The story describes how Mrs Mashaka, the Geography and the Environment teacher, took her class to the Serengeti National Park, divided them into three groups to record the animals, birds and insects seen, and the class reported their findings back at school.
sla_notes_illustrations: From the story: the animals seen were lions, elephants, giraffes, buffaloes, zebras, antelopes and monkeys; the birds were eagles, ostriches, flamingos, crows and woodpeckers; the insects included bees, wasps, grasshoppers, ants, tsetse flies and butterflies.
sla_notes_daily_life: Reading aloud clearly and answering questions about a class trip helps a pupil report on their own school trips or activities to their family.
sla_exercise: What subject does Mrs Mashaka teach?::She teaches Geography and the Environment.||What was the first group asked to do?::The first group was asked to write the names of animals.||What was the second group asked to do?::The second group was asked to write the names of birds.||What animals did the class see at the Serengeti?::They saw lions, elephants, giraffes, buffaloes, zebras, antelopes and monkeys.||What insects did the class see at the Serengeti?::They saw bees, wasps, grasshoppers, ants, tsetse flies and butterflies.

sla_notes_intro: A pronoun is a word that replaces a noun. The unit introduces the English personal pronouns that pupils will use when speaking and writing, such as I, you, he, she, it, we and they.
sla_notes_details: Singular pronouns are I, you, she, he and it, while plural pronouns are we, you and they, as shown in the book's singular/plural table.
sla_notes_illustrations: Pronoun song: 'A pronoun is a word that replaces a noun x 2 / you or I or it or she / them or us or her or me / theirs or ours or we / mine or hers or him or he'. Table: Singular - I, you, she, he, it; Plural - we, you, they, they, they.
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil uses 'he' or 'she' instead of repeating a friend's name over and over when telling the family about a classmate.
sla_exercise: What word replaces a noun?::A pronoun.||Is 'she' a singular or plural pronoun?::Singular.||Is 'they' a singular or plural pronoun?::Plural.||Give two singular pronouns from the song.::I and she (also he, it, you).

sla_name: Using pronouns orally in the interview with a farmer dialogue
sla_method: Dialogue role play and gap filling
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly fills in the missing pronouns in the dialogue and role-plays it with a partner using the right pronouns for the speaker and listener.
sla_teaching_aids: Dialogue chart: An interview with a farmer|Audio recording of the dialogue|Role play cards
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Pronouns are used in conversation to refer to the speaker (I), the listener (you) or things already mentioned (they), so that people do not keep repeating names, as shown in 'An interview with a farmer' between Luta and Maswi.
sla_notes_details: In the dialogue, Luta uses 'I' to talk about himself buying cows, Maswi uses 'you' to answer Luta, and both use 'they' to refer to the cows already mentioned.
sla_notes_illustrations: Completed dialogue: Luta: I'm Luta. I want to buy cows. Do you have any? Maswi: Yes, I do. Luta: I would like to buy two bulls. Can I get them? Maswi: Yes, you can. Maswi: You will pay four hundred thousand shillings for a small one. Luta: Where are they? Can I see them? Maswi: Sure, you will see them on the farm. Maswi: Here they are. If you like them, pay me and have them.
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil at a real market or farm uses 'I' to say what they want and 'you' to ask the seller a question, just like Luta and Maswi.
sla_exercise: Who says 'I want to buy cows' in the dialogue?::Luta, referring to himself.||Which pronoun does Maswi use to tell Luta he is allowed to get the bulls?::You (Yes, you can).||Which pronoun replaces 'the cows' in 'Can I see them?'::Them.||Fill in: 'Here _____ are' (about the cows).::they

sla_notes_intro: A pronoun replaces a noun that has already been mentioned so that a story does not sound repetitive, as practised in the story about Mtakuya Primary School's sports day.
sla_notes_details: 'It' replaces 'sports day', 'they' replaces 'pupils', 'he' replaces 'James', 'she' replaces 'Natalia', and 'we' replaces 'our team', showing how the correct pronoun depends on the noun just mentioned.
sla_notes_illustrations: Completed story: '...It is always held on the last Friday of the term... They were waiting for the inter-class competitions... He was the team captain. I was in the netball team... She is our best scorer. She scored many goals for our team, and the netball match was tough, and we lost to Standard Two... It ended up 2 to 1.'
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil retelling what happened at school uses 'he' or 'she' for a classmate and 'it' for the event, instead of repeating the same name many times.
sla_exercise: Which pronoun replaces 'sports day' in 'It is always held on the last Friday'?::It.||Which pronoun replaces 'James' in 'He was the team captain'?::He.||Which pronoun replaces 'Natalia' in 'She is our best scorer'?::She.||Which pronoun is used for 'our team' in 'we lost to Standard Two'?::We.

sla_notes_intro: When writing about a person, animal or group already named in a sentence, the next sentence uses a pronoun such as she, he, it, we or they instead of repeating the noun.

sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil writing a letter about their aunt who is a doctor writes 'She works for the hospital' instead of repeating 'my aunt' in every sentence.
sla_exercise: Jamila is my best friend. _____ loves cooking. Which pronoun fits?::She.||Peter is going to the birthday party. _____ is going with Baraka. Which pronoun fits?::He.||Look at the cow under the tree. _____ is big and fat. Which pronoun fits?::It.||Naomi and Sonia went to the playground. _____ went to play netball. sla_teaching_aids: Possession song audio (John has a star)|Have/Has sentence table chart
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Possession is a state of having something. Have is used with I, you, we and they, while has is used with he, she and it, as introduced at the start of the unit on expressing possession.
sla_notes_details: The song shows 'has' going with a single owner (John has a star, Ely has a star) and 'have' going with I, you and we, while the table practises I have a book, You have a ruler, We have a pen, They have sweets, He has a watch, She has a pencil.
sla_notes_illustrations: Song: 'John has a star. Ely has a star. I have a hat. You have a hat, We have hats, and they have stars.' Table sentences: I have a book. You have a ruler. We have a pen. They have sweets. He has a watch.
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil describing their family says 'My father has a bicycle' but 'My brothers and I have bicycles', choosing has or have correctly for each person.
sla_exercise: Which word goes with 'John' - has or have?::Has.||Which word goes with 'I' - has or have?::Have.||Complete: 'We _____ hats' (has/have).::have||Complete: 'He _____ a watch' (has/have).::has

sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil answers comprehension questions about the giraffe passage using has or doesn't have correctly to describe what the giraffe possesses.
sla_teaching_aids: Giraffe passage chart|Picture of a giraffe
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Has is used to say what a single animal or person possesses, as shown in the passage where the giraffe has a long neck, a small head, short ears, long legs and a calf.
sla_notes_details: The giraffe has a long neck, two long front legs, two strong hind legs, and a beautiful skin with brown spots; the giraffe has a calf, and the calf has a short tail and brown spots too.
sla_notes_illustrations: Passage: 'The giraffe is a beautiful animal. It has a long neck. The giraffe has a small head with short ears... The giraffe has a calf. The calf has a very short tail and brown spots.' Answers: Yes, the giraffe has a long neck. No, the giraffe doesn't have a short neck. Yes, the giraffe has a calf. Yes, the calf has a short tail.
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil describing their pet dog at home says 'My dog has short legs and a long tail', using has the same way the book describes the giraffe.
sla_exercise: Does the giraffe have a long neck?::Yes, the giraffe has a long neck.||Does the giraffe have short legs?::No, the giraffe doesn't have short legs.||Does the giraffe have a calf?::Yes, the giraffe has a calf.||Does the giraffe's calf have a short tail?::Yes, the giraffe's calf has a short tail.

sla_notes_intro: Have is used with 'I' and 'you' when asking and answering about what someone possesses, as in the dialogue where Mrs Mrisho asks Juma 'Do you have fresh mangoes?' and Juma answers 'Yes, I have very good ones'.
sla_notes_details: Juma has mangoes, bananas and oranges from his own stall, but he does not have pineapples himself; his neighbour has pineapples instead, showing has for a single seller and have for 'I' and 'they'.
sla_notes_illustrations: Dialogue: 'Do you have fresh mangoes?' 'Yes, I have very good ones from Tanga.' 'Do you have pineapples?' 'Oh, no! I don't have any. But I can get them for you from my neighbour.' 'Yes! I have very good bananas from Morogoro and very sweet oranges from Muheza.'

sla_notes_details: In the poultry farm story, 'my parents have a poultry farm' and 'they have many hens', but 'my white hen has ten chicks'; in the picture practice, 'the monkey has a long tail' and 'this boy has a bag', using has for one owner.

sla_notes_intro: Routines are the things or actions we do regularly. Pupils learn to talk about things that are done regularly using appropriate verb forms in the simple present tense.
sla_notes_details: The simple present tense is used with time expressions such as 'every morning', 'every day', 'every week' and 'every evening' to show actions that happen regularly, for example 'I wash my face every morning' and 'I comb my hair every morning'.
sla_notes_illustrations: From the song: 'This is the way I comb my hair, comb my hair, comb my hair. This is the way I comb my hair, every day in the morning.' Also: 'This is the way I wash my face... every day so early in the morning' and 'This is the way I ride my bicycle... every day in the evening.'
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil can tell a friend what he or she does every morning before coming to school, such as washing the face and combing the hair.
sla_exercise: What do you do every morning?::I wash my face and comb my hair every morning.||How often does she comb her hair that way?::She combs her hair that way every day in the morning.||When does she wash her face that way?::She washes her face that way every day so early in the morning.||How often does she ride her bicycle that way?::She rides her bicycle that way every day in the evening.

sla_notes_intro: Reading practice builds on the routines learnt in Activity 1 by presenting a full passage, 'My day', in which Nasha describes her typical daily routine in the simple present tense.
sla_notes_details: The passage uses sequencing words such as 'First', 'Next', 'At', and 'Between... and...' together with simple present tense verbs to order the events of the day, for example 'I wake up at 6:00 am and brush my teeth' and 'I attend lessons from 8:00 am to 4:00 pm.'
sla_notes_illustrations: From 'My day': 'Hello! My name is Nasha. I am nine years old... First, I wake up at 6:00 am and brush my teeth. Next, I have a bath at 6:15 am and drink tea at 6:30 am. At 7:00 am, I take my school bag and go to school... At 5:00 pm, I do domestic chores. I eat dinner at 8:00 pm... At 8:30 pm, I go to sleep.'
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil can compare his or her own morning routine, such as the time of waking up and going to school, with Nasha's routine in the passage.
sla_exercise: What does Nasha do first after waking up?::She brushes her teeth.||What does Nasha do after drinking tea?::She takes her school bag and goes to school.||What time does Nasha go to sleep?::She goes to sleep at 8:30 pm.||What time do the lessons end?::The lessons end at 4:00 pm.

sla_notes_intro: Writing practice moves pupils from reading about someone else's routine to writing their own daily routine, filling in blanks with the correct simple present tense verb forms and personal details such as name, age and school.
sla_notes_details: Pupils complete a guided paragraph describing waking up, washing, having breakfast, going to school, attending lessons, resting, doing chores, eating dinner, doing homework and going to sleep, all in the simple present tense.
sla_notes_illustrations: From 'My daily routine': 'My name is ______. I am ______ years old. I am in Standard ______ at ______ Primary School... Every day, I ______ early in the morning at 6:00 am. After waking up, I ______ my teeth and ______ my face or have a bath.'

I am nine years old.||Complete: 'Every day, I ______ early in the morning at 6:00 am.'::Every day, I wake up early in the morning at 6:00 am.||Complete: 'After waking up, I ______ my teeth.'::After waking up, I brush my teeth.||Complete: 'I eat dinner at ______.'::I eat dinner at 8:00 pm.

sla_name: Describing ongoing activities using present continuous tense
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly describes actions happening at the moment of speech using the present continuous tense, such as 'He is dancing' and 'She is cooking.'
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of people performing actions|Word box: teaching, cleaning, singing, sweeping, beating, opening, reading, running|Subject-verb-object practice table
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Ongoing activities are actions or events happening at the moment of speech. Pupils learn the appropriate verb form, 'is/am/are + verb-ing', to describe activities happening right now.
sla_notes_details: The present continuous tense is formed with the verb 'to be' (am, is, are) followed by the main verb ending in '-ing'. For example: 'I am learning English', 'We are sweeping the floor', 'She is swimming', 'He is eating breakfast.'
sla_notes_illustrations: From the pictures: 'He is dancing. He is riding a bicycle. She is cooking. He is watering the flowers. She is washing clothes. She is mopping the floor. He is reading a book. He is watching cartoons.'
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil can describe what a family member is doing right now at home, for example 'My mother is cooking' or 'My father is watering the flowers.'
sla_exercise: What is he doing? (bicycle picture)::He is riding a bicycle.||What is she doing? (kitchen picture)::She is cooking.||What is she doing? (floor picture)::She is mopping the floor.||Construct a sentence using 'is reading'.::He is reading a book.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English Language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Express routines and ongoing activities in school and home contexts (target: simple present tense, present continuous tense)
sla_name: Forming questions about ongoing activities in present continuous tense
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly fills in present continuous tense verb forms and changes statements about ongoing activities into questions using 'what' and 'where'.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of Hamisi eating a mango and getting sick|Sentence strips for arranging the story in order|Question-formation worksheet
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Building on ongoing activities, pupils practise supplying the correct present continuous verb form in gaps and transforming present continuous statements into questions.
sla_notes_details: To form a question in the present continuous tense, the verb 'to be' moves before the subject, and a question word such as 'what' or 'where' may be added, for example the statement 'His parents are taking him to hospital' becomes 'Where are his parents taking him?'
sla_notes_illustrations: From the story of Hamisi: 'Hamisi is picking a mango under the tree. He is eating the mango without washing it. He is crying because of a stomach ache. His parents are taking him to hospital.' Question example: 'He is crying.' becomes 'What is he crying about?'
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil can ask a classmate a question about what he or she is doing right now, such as 'What are you reading?'
sla_exercise: Fill in: My younger sister is ______ (eat) a cake.::My younger sister is eating a cake.||Fill in: My mother is ______ (cook) in the kitchen.::My mother is cooking in the kitchen.||Change to a question: 'He is eating a mango.'::What is he eating?||Change to a question: 'Hamisi is picking a mango.'::What is Hamisi picking?

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English Language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Use conjunctions in oral and written contexts (target: and, but)
sla_name: Joining sentences with the conjunction 'and' orally
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil orally joins two simple sentences of the same status into one sentence using 'and', such as combining 'I like English' and 'I like Kiswahili' into 'I like English and Kiswahili.'
sla_teaching_aids: Sentence pair cards|Example chart showing 'I like English and Kiswahili'|Pictures for oral practice
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Conjunctions are words used to join words or sentences together. This lesson introduces the conjunction 'and', used to connect simple sentences of the same status.
sla_notes_details: When two sentences share the same subject and a similar type of idea, they can be joined with 'and', often by combining the repeated part, for example 'I like English. I like Kiswahili.' becomes 'I like English and Kiswahili.'
sla_notes_illustrations: From the book: '(i) I like English. I like Kiswahili. -> I like English and Kiswahili.' '(iv) John is wearing a white shirt. Sarah is wearing a white shirt. -> John and Sarah are wearing a white shirt.' '(vi) Asha likes rope skipping. Asha likes netball. -> Asha likes rope skipping and netball.'
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil can use 'and' to tell a friend two things he or she likes, such as 'I like ugali and beans.'
sla_exercise: Join with 'and': 'John likes English. John likes Kiswahili.'::John likes English and Kiswahili.||Join with 'and': 'Sarah has a school bag. John has a school bag.'::Sarah and John have a school bag.||Join with 'and': 'I am healthy. I am happy.'::I am healthy and happy.||Join with 'and': 'I have one sister. I have one brother.'::I have one sister and one brother.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English Language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Use conjunctions in oral and written contexts (target: and, but)
sla_name: Joining sentences with the conjunction 'and' in writing
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly writes joined sentences using 'and' to combine two related written sentences into one, such as 'Juma hunts birds and bats.'
sla_teaching_aids: Worksheet with sentence pairs to join|Model sentence 'Juma hunts birds and bats'|Exercise book
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson extends oral use of 'and' into writing, where pupils practise combining two written sentences of the same status into a single correctly punctuated sentence.
sla_notes_details: In writing, the second occurrence of the repeated subject or verb is usually dropped when the sentences are joined, for example 'Our class has fifteen girls. Our class has twenty boys.' becomes 'Our class has fifteen girls and twenty boys.'
sla_notes_illustrations: From the book: 'Juma hunts birds. Juma hunts bats. -> Juma hunts birds and bats.' 'The ducks are eating rice. The hens are eating rice. -> The ducks and the hens are eating rice.' 'The carpenter is fixing the door. The carpenter is fixing the window. -> The carpenter is fixing the door and the window.'
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil can write a sentence about chores at home joined with 'and', such as 'We have a bath and eat breakfast in the morning.'
sla_exercise: Join with 'and': 'Maria visits her grandmother on Sundays. Maria visits her uncle on Sundays.'::Maria visits her grandmother and her uncle on Sundays.||Join with 'and': 'Our mother likes ugali. Our father likes ugali.'::Our mother and our father like ugali.||Join with 'and': 'We have a bath in the morning. We eat breakfast in the morning.'::We have a bath and eat breakfast in the morning.||Join with 'and': 'The doctor is examining the child. The doctor is examining the mother.'::The doctor is examining the child and the mother.

specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Use conjunctions in oral and written contexts (target: and, but)
sla_name: Joining contrasting sentences with the conjunction 'but' orally
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil orally joins two contrasting sentences into one using 'but', such as combining 'I like football' and 'I don't like netball' into 'I like football, but I don't like netball.'
sla_teaching_aids: Sentence pair cards showing contrasting ideas|Example chart 'I like football, but I don't like netball'|Pictures for oral practice
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This lesson introduces the conjunction 'but', used to connect two ideas that contrast with each other, unlike 'and' which connects similar ideas.
sla_notes_details: When the second sentence contrasts with or contradicts the first, the sentences are joined with 'but' and a comma is placed before it, for example 'I like football. I don't like netball.' becomes 'I like football, but I don't like netball.'
sla_notes_illustrations: From the book: '(i) I like football. I don't like netball. -> I like football, but I don't like netball.' '(iv) Sarah likes netball. Sarah does not like football. -> Sarah likes netball, but she does not like football.' '(vii) Neema likes netball. Jane likes football. -> Neema likes netball, but Jane likes football.'
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil can use 'but' to tell a friend about two contrasting preferences, such as 'I like rice, but I don't like beans.'
sla_exercise: Join with 'but': 'I like netball. I don't like football.'::I like netball, but I don't like football.||Join with 'but': 'John likes football. John does not like netball.'::John likes football, but he does not like netball.||Join with 'but': 'I like rope skipping. I don't like football.'::I like rope skipping, but I don't like football.||Join with 'but': 'My parents are rich. I am not happy.'::My parents are rich, but I am not happy.

sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly writes joined sentences using 'but' to combine two contrasting written sentences into one, such as 'Juma hunts birds, but he does not hunt bats.'

sla_notes_intro: This lesson extends oral use of 'but' into writing, where pupils practise combining two contrasting written sentences into a single correctly punctuated sentence using 'but'.
sla_notes_details: In writing, when the two sentences share the same subject, the subject in the second part is usually replaced with a pronoun after 'but', for example 'The carpenter is fixing the door. The carpenter is not fixing the window.' becomes 'The carpenter is fixing the door, but he is not fixing the window.'
sla_notes_illustrations: From the book: 'Juma hunts birds. Juma does not hunt bats. -> Juma hunts birds, but he does not hunt bats.' 'The ducks are eating rice. The hens are not eating rice. -> The ducks are eating rice, but the hens are not.' 'Our class has fifteen girls. Our class does not have twenty boys. -> Our class has fifteen girls, but it does not have twenty boys.'
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil can write about home life using 'but' to show contrast, such as 'We have a bath in the morning, but we do not eat breakfast in the morning.'
sla_exercise: Join with 'but': 'Maria visits her grandmother on Sunday. Maria does not visit her uncle on Sunday.'::Maria visits her grandmother on Sunday, but she does not visit her uncle.||Join with 'but': 'Our mother likes ugali. Our father does not like ugali.'::Our mother likes ugali, but our father does not like it.||Join with 'but': 'We have a bath in the morning. We do not eat breakfast in the morning.'::We have a bath in the morning, but we do not eat breakfast.||Join with 'but': 'The doctor is examining the child. The doctor is not examining the mother.'::The doctor is examining the child, but he is not examining the mother.

sla_name: Identifying and reading two-syllable picture words
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly reads aloud at least five of the six two-syllable words shown under the pictures (mango, carrot, onion, toothbrush, orange, cabbage) with the syllable break in the right place.
sla_teaching_aids: Flashcards with pictures and words|Picture cards of fruits and vegetables|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A syllable is a single unit of sound in a word. Many everyday words we see in pictures, such as the names of fruits and vegetables, are made up of two syllables. Reading the word below a picture and clapping out its syllables helps pupils hear the two beats in the word.
sla_notes_details: Two-syllable picture words from the book: man-go, car-rot, on-ion, tooth-brush, or-ange, cab-bage. Pupils look at each picture, say the word, then clap once for each syllable to confirm it has two beats.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example: the picture of a mango is labelled 'mango', read and clapped as man-go (2 claps). The picture of a toothbrush is labelled 'toothbrush', read and clapped as tooth-brush (2 claps).
sla_notes_daily_life: Pupils use these same two-syllable words like carrot, onion and cabbage when they help their parents name vegetables while shopping or cooking at home.
sla_exercise: How many syllables does the word 'mango' have?::It has two syllables, man-go.||Read aloud the word under the toothbrush picture.::toothbrush, read as tooth-brush.||Name one two-syllable vegetable word from the pictures.::carrot (or onion, or cabbage).

sla_name: Reading two-syllable words: notice, careful, pencil, today, learning, spider, outside, prevent, window
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil reads aloud, with correct syllable breaks, at least six of the nine listed two-syllable words without hesitation.
sla_teaching_aids: Word list chart (rows 1-3)|Flashcards|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Two-syllable words are broken into two clear sound parts. In the book's practice list, words such as no-tice, care-ful and pen-cil show how the first syllable is stressed while the second follows smoothly.
sla_notes_details: Word list from the book, rows 1-3: no-tice, care-ful, pen-cil, to-day, learn-ing, spi-der, out-side, pre-vent, win-dow. Pupils practise reading each word aloud, pausing briefly at the hyphen to hear both syllables.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example: 'notice' is read as no-tice; 'today' is read as to-day; 'spider' is read as spi-der; 'window' is read as win-dow.
sla_notes_daily_life: Pupils use words like 'today', 'outside' and 'window' every day when talking about the weather, playtime, or their classroom.
sla_exercise: Read aloud the word 'notice' and say its syllables.::notice, read as no-tice.||How many syllables does 'window' have?::Two syllables, win-dow.||Read the word 'outside' syllable by syllable.::out-side.

sla_notes_intro: This SLA continues the book's practice list, guiding pupils to read more two-syllable words correctly after hearing the teacher model the pronunciation first.
sla_notes_details: Word list from the book, rows 4-5: soft-ly, pur-pose, rab-bit, re-ceive, lap-top, mon-day. The teacher reads each word first, then pupils repeat it, breaking it into its two syllables.

sla_notes_daily_life: Pupils use the word 'vocabulary' when their teacher talks about learning new words, and 'hippopotamus' when describing animals they have seen or heard about.

sla_name: Reading aloud the story 'A bad man paid the price'
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil reads aloud a paragraph of the story 'A bad man paid the price' fluently, with correct pronunciation, stress and pacing.
sla_teaching_aids: Pupils' book story text|Chalkboard|Flashcards of key words (hospital, bench, doctor, policeman, corruption)
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Reading aloud grade-level texts means pupils practise fluent, expressive reading of a full story, not just single words. The story 'A bad man paid the price' tells of Tupendane, who was taken to hospital and waited with other patients while a man named Toyo bribed the doctor to be seen first.
sla_notes_details: The story: Tupendane was sick and taken to hospital, where she and other patients waited on a bench for the doctor. A man named Toyo arrived, shook hands with the doctor to bribe him, and was called in ahead of the queue. The patients shouted in protest, Tupendane's mother called the police, and a policeman arrested both Toyo and the doctor. Tupendane's mother told the patients, 'Corruption is the enemy of justice!'
sla_notes_illustrations: Illustration from the book text: '...the doctor shouted, "Toyo, come in." It was clear that he had bribed the doctor... Tupendane's mother called the police... He arrested Toyo and the doctor.' Pupils practise reading this passage aloud with expression, especially the quoted speech.
sla_notes_daily_life: Pupils learn that waiting one's turn fairly, such as in a queue at a clinic or shop, is important and that bribing to skip the queue is wrong.
sla_exercise: Where was Tupendane taken because she was sick?::She was taken to hospital.||What did Toyo do to be seen before the other patients?::He bribed the doctor by pretending to shake his hand.||Who arrested Toyo and the doctor?::A policeman arrested them.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Read a variety of simple texts appropriately
learning_activity_name: Read aloud a variety of grade-level texts
sla_name: Answering comprehension questions on 'A bad man paid the price'
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil answers at least four of the six comprehension questions from the story correctly in complete oral sentences.
sla_teaching_aids: Pupils' book story text|Chalkboard with question list
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: After reading a story aloud, pupils must show they understood it by answering questions orally. The book provides six questions on 'A bad man paid the price' to check comprehension and vocabulary, including the meanings of 'enemy' and 'justice'.
sla_notes_details: The six book questions: (i) Why was Tupendane taken to hospital? (ii) Who pretended to shake hands with the doctor? (iii) Why were Toyo and the doctor arrested? (iv) What is your opinion about corruption? (v) What is the meaning of the word enemy? (vi) What is the meaning of the word justice?
sla_notes_illustrations: Example answers: Tupendane was taken to hospital because she was sick. Toyo pretended to shake hands with the doctor to bribe him. Toyo and the doctor were arrested because of corruption. Tupendane's mother said, 'Corruption is the enemy of justice!'
sla_notes_daily_life: Pupils apply this by explaining to family members why bribery and unfair queue-jumping, such as at a hospital or bus stop, are wrong.
sla_exercise: Why was Tupendane taken to hospital?::Because she was sick.||Why were Toyo and the doctor arrested?::Because Toyo had bribed the doctor to be seen ahead of the other patients, which is corruption.||What is the meaning of the word 'justice' as used in the story?::Fairness, or people being treated rightly and equally.

sla_name: Reading aloud the story 'Two friends went fishing'
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil reads aloud a section of 'Two friends went fishing' clearly and fluently, correctly pronouncing the dialogue between Monde and Tutu.
sla_teaching_aids: Pupils' book story text|Chalkboard|Fishing rod picture card
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This is a second grade-level story for reading aloud practice, about two friends, Monde and Tutu, who went fishing at the river and caught a very big fish together.
sla_notes_details: The story: Monde and his friend Tutu went fishing at the river, each with a fishing rod. Monde caught a very big fish and screamed for Tutu to come and help. Tutu ran over, grabbed the rod, and helped pull the fish out of the water. Monde took the fish home and told his mother how they caught it together, and said he would cook it.
sla_notes_illustrations: Illustration from the book text: 'Monde caught a very big fish. He screamed, "Tutuuu! Tutuuu! Come! I have caught a big fish." Tutu ran towards Monde. He grabbed the fishing rod and started pulling the fish out of water.' Pupils practise reading this excitedly, as Monde would have shouted it.
sla_notes_daily_life: Pupils relate this to times they have helped a friend or family member with a task, such as carrying something heavy together.
sla_exercise: Where did Monde and Tutu go fishing?::At the river.||What did Monde do when he caught the big fish?::He screamed for Tutu to come and help him.||What did Monde plan to do with the fish?::He planned to cook it.

sla_notes_intro: As with the first story, pupils answer questions orally to demonstrate understanding of 'Two friends went fishing'. The book asks three questions focused on the sequence of events.
sla_notes_details: The three book questions: (i) What did Monde catch? (ii) Why did Monde scream? (iii) What did Tutu do?
sla_notes_illustrations: Example answers: Monde caught a very big fish. Monde screamed because he was excited and wanted Tutu to come and see the big fish. Tutu ran to Monde, grabbed the fishing rod, and helped pull the fish out of the water.
sla_notes_daily_life: Pupils apply this skill by retelling, in their own words, a time they or a friend caught, found, or achieved something exciting.
sla_exercise: What did Monde catch?::A very big fish.||Why did Monde scream?::Because he was excited and wanted Tutu to come and see the big fish he had caught.||What did Tutu do to help Monde?::He grabbed the fishing rod and helped pull the fish out of the water.

specific_competence_name: Read a variety of simple texts appropriately

sla_name: Reading aloud with correct stress and intonation, and acting out dialogue

sla_notes_intro: The unit's introduction explains that reading aloud develops the ability to hear, pronounce and place word stress and intonation appropriately. Acting out dialogue, such as Monde calling excitedly to Tutu, helps pupils practise this expressive reading in a natural, spoken way.
sla_notes_details: Dialogue from the book: Monde: 'Tutuuu! Tutuuu! Come! A big fish, come!' Tutu: 'Here I am. Wow! It's real big. Let me help you.' Monde: 'Wow! What a big fish! I'm taking it home, Tutu. Thanks.' In groups of two or three, pupils take turns acting out these lines aloud.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example: pupils practise stressing 'Tutuuu!' loudly and excitedly, just as Monde would call out when he needed urgent help, and use a rising tone for 'Wow! What a big fish!' to show surprise.
sla_notes_daily_life: Pupils use expressive stress and intonation when calling out to friends or family in real, exciting situations, such as sharing good news.
sla_exercise: Who says 'Tutuuu! Tutuuu! Come! A big fish, come!' in the dialogue?::Monde says it.||How should Monde's call to Tutu be read aloud?::Loudly and excitedly, since he is calling for urgent help.||What does Tutu say when he sees the fish?::'Here I am. sla_name: Identifying short vowel sounds /I/, /ae/, /e/ and /o/ in words
sla_method: Sort the words / Instructional routines (touch and say)
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly reads aloud a list of words with the short vowel sounds /I/, /ae/, /e/ and /o/ without mispronouncing the vowel.
sla_teaching_aids: Wallchart of short vowel words|Word cards (ship, mat, bed, pot)|Pupil's book Unit Eight
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Spoken English has certain basic features that differentiate it from other forms of delivery, including differences in pronunciation between words. Short vowel sounds such as /I/, /ae/, /e/ and /o/ are heard in many common English words and pupils must learn to recognise and pronounce them correctly.
sla_notes_details: The short vowel /I/ is heard in words such as ship, lip and pin; /ae/ is heard in mat, cat and hat; /e/ is heard in bed, let and bet; /o/ is heard in pot, lock and mop. Pupils read the words after the teacher, repeating each sound clearly.
sla_notes_illustrations: Words from Activity 1(a): ship, lip, pin, dip (short /I/); mat, cat, hat, bag (short /ae/); bed, let, bet (short /e/); pot, lock, mop, check, top, order (short /o/).
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil uses correct short vowel pronunciation when telling a friend that 'the cat sat on the mat' so the message is clearly understood.
sla_exercise: Read aloud: ship, lip, pin.::These words all have the short vowel sound /I/.||Read aloud: mat, cat, hat.::These words all have the short vowel sound /ae/.||Which word has the same vowel sound as 'bed': 'let' or 'boot'?::'let' has the same short vowel sound /e/ as 'bed'.||Read aloud: pot, lock, mop.::These words all have the short vowel sound /o/.

sla_name: Reading words with the short vowel sounds /u^/ and /u/
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil pronounces words containing /u^/ and /u/, such as cut and full, with the correct short vowel sound.
sla_teaching_aids: Word cards (cut, mud, full, put)|Wallchart of short vowel words|Pupil's book Unit Eight
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Some short vowel sounds are easily confused by learners, especially /u^/ as in 'cut' and /u/ as in 'full'. Careful listening and repetition after the teacher helps pupils to hear the difference.
sla_notes_details: The short vowel /u^/ is heard in cut, mud, run and hug. The short vowel /u/ is heard in full, put, pull and bull. Pupils read the words after the teacher and then read them aloud independently.
sla_notes_illustrations: Words from Activity 1(a): cut, mud, run, hug (short /u^/); full, put, pull, bull (short /u/).
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing the /u/ sound helps a pupil say 'put the bag on the table' correctly instead of confusing it with a similar-sounding word.
sla_exercise: Read aloud: cut, mud, run, hug.::These words have the short vowel sound /u^/.||Read aloud: full, put, pull, bull.::These words have the short vowel sound /u/.||Which word means the opposite of 'empty' and has the /u/ sound?::'full' has the sound /u/ and means the opposite of empty.||Say a sentence using the word 'cut'.::Example: He cut the mango into three pieces.

sla_name: Identifying long vowel sounds /i:/ and /u:/ in words
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil distinguishes and reads aloud words containing the long vowel sounds /i:/ and /u:/, such as heap and fool.
sla_teaching_aids: Wallchart of long vowel words|Word cards (heap, leap, fool, boot)|Pupil's book Unit Eight
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Long vowel sounds are held for longer than short vowel sounds. The sounds /i:/ and /u:/ are examples of long vowels found in many English words, and recognising them is part of the basic features of spoken English.
sla_notes_details: The long vowel /i:/ is heard in heap, leap and feel. The long vowel /u:/ is heard in fool, boot and pool. Pupils read the words after the teacher, holding the vowel sound longer than in short vowel words.
sla_notes_illustrations: Words from Activity 2(a): heap, leap, feel (long /i:/); fool, boot, pool (long /u:/).
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil uses the long /u:/ sound correctly when reading a sign that says 'swimming pool' at school.
sla_exercise: Read aloud: heap, leap, feel.::These words have the long vowel sound /i:/.||Read aloud: fool, boot, pool.::These words have the long vowel sound /u:/.||Which word rhymes with 'cool' and has the /u:/ sound?::'fool', 'boot' and 'pool' rhyme with 'cool'.||Is the vowel sound in 'feel' short or long?::It is a long vowel sound, /i:/.

sla_name: Reading words with the long vowel sounds /a:/ and /e:/
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil reads aloud words containing /a:/ and /e:/, such as park and girl, with the correct long vowel sound.
sla_teaching_aids: Word cards (park, part, girl, bird)|Wallchart of long vowel words|Pupil's book Unit Eight
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The long vowels /a:/ and /e:/ are also common features of spoken English. /a:/ is a long, open back sound while /e:/ is a long, central sound heard before letters such as 'ir' and 'ur'.
sla_notes_details: The long vowel /a:/ is heard in park, part and bark. The long vowel /e:/ is heard in girl, bird and church. Pupils read the words after the teacher, then read the additional words third, heard, mark, dark, farm, arm, word and sword.
sla_notes_illustrations: Words from Activity 2(a) and (b): park, part, bark, mark, dark, farm, arm (long /a:/); girl, bird, church, third, heard, word (long /e:/).
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil pronounces 'bird' and 'church' correctly when describing a bird singing near the church on the way to school.
sla_exercise: Read aloud: park, part, bark.::These words have the long vowel sound /a:/.||Read aloud: girl, bird, church.::These words have the long vowel sound /e:/.||Which of these has the same vowel sound as 'bird': 'third' or 'top'?::'third' has the same long vowel sound /e:/ as 'bird'.||Read aloud: farm, arm, word.::'farm' and 'arm' have the long vowel /a:/, while 'word' has the long vowel /e:/.

sla_name: Distinguishing minimal pairs of short and long vowels (ship/sheep, full/fool, dip/deep)
sla_method: Sort the words / Pair and compare
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly identifies whether a word has a short or long vowel sound when given word pairs such as ship/sheep and full/fool.
sla_teaching_aids: Word pair cards (ship/sheep, full/fool, dip/deep)|Wallchart contrasting short and long vowels|Pupil's book Unit Eight
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Some English words look and sound similar but differ only in the length of the vowel sound, such as 'ship' (short /I/) and 'sheep' (long /i:/). Recognising this difference is an important basic feature of spoken English.
sla_notes_details: Pupils compare words from Activity 1 and Activity 2 in pairs, for example ship/sheep, full/fool, and dip/deep, noticing that the long vowel word is held for longer.
sla_notes_illustrations: From Activities 1, 2 and 4: 'ship' (short /I/) contrasted with the sentence 'I saw a sheep on the ship'; 'full' (short /u/) contrasted with 'fool' (long /u:/); 'dip' (short /I/) contrasted with 'deep' (long /i:/).
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing the difference between 'ship' and 'sheep' helps a pupil avoid confusion when listening to a story about animals travelling on a boat.
sla_exercise: Which word has a short vowel sound: 'ship' or 'sheep'?::'ship' has the short vowel sound /I/, while 'sheep' has the long vowel sound /i:/.||Which word has a short vowel sound: 'full' or 'fool'?::'full' has the short vowel /u/, while 'fool' has the long vowel /u:/.||Say the pair 'dip' and 'deep'. Which is longer?::'deep' has the long vowel /i:/, so it is held longer than 'dip'.||Use 'ship' and 'sheep' in one sentence.::Example: I saw a sheep on the ship.

sla_notes_intro: Activity 3 of the pupil's book presents two columns of words, one with long vowel sounds and one with short vowel sounds, so that pupils can compare and practise both types side by side.

sla_notes_intro: Fluency in spoken English means being able to pronounce words correctly and quickly, without hesitating over each sound. Pupils practise reading long vowel words repeatedly to build speed.

sla_name: Reading simple sentences with short and long vowel words
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil reads simple sentences containing short and long vowel words, such as 'I saw a sheep on the ship,' clearly and correctly.
sla_teaching_aids: Sentence strips (I saw a ship. / I saw a sheep on the ship.)|Wallchart of sentences|Pupil's book Unit Eight
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Activity 4(a) of the pupil's book presents short sentences that combine words with short and long vowel sounds, giving pupils practice reading whole sentences, not just single words.
sla_notes_details: Pupils read sentences such as 'I saw a ship,' 'I saw a sheep on the ship,' 'Tutu likes to bet,' 'The pot is full,' and 'The thief is a fool,' paying attention to the vowel sound in each key word.
sla_notes_illustrations: From Activity 4(a): (i) I saw a ship. (ii) I saw a sheep on the ship. (v) The pot is full. (vi) The thief is a fool. (ix) He cut the mango into three pieces.
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil uses these sentence patterns to describe things they see, for example telling a friend 'I saw a sheep on the way to school.'
sla_exercise: Read aloud: 'I saw a sheep on the ship.'::Pupil reads the sentence correctly, pronouncing 'sheep' with a long vowel and 'ship' with a short vowel.||Read aloud: 'The pot is full.'::Pupil reads the sentence correctly, pronouncing 'pot' and 'full' with short vowels.||Read aloud: 'The thief is a fool.'::Pupil reads the sentence correctly, pronouncing 'fool' with a long vowel.||Read aloud: 'He cut the mango into three pieces.'::Pupil reads the sentence correctly, pronouncing 'cut' with a short vowel.

sla_name: Reciting the poem 'The sailor wants to sail' for intonation and fluency
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil recites the poem 'The sailor wants to sail' aloud with correct pronunciation, rhythm and intonation.
sla_teaching_aids: Poem chart (The sailor wants to sail)|Pupil's book Unit Eight
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Activity 4(b) presents a short poem about a sailor, giving pupils a chance to practise intonation and rhythm in spoken English while reading connected verse rather than single sentences.
sla_notes_details: The poem describes a sailor who sees a whale, a big wave and rain, and dense clouds that stop him from sailing. Pupils recite it line by line, then as a whole poem, focusing on rhythm and clear pronunciation.
sla_notes_illustrations: From Activity 4(b): 'The sailor wants to sail. He sees a whale on the shore, With a big chain on its tail. Then a big wave and rain come. Dense clouds put them in the shade. The sailor is dismayed. There is no sailing!'
sla_notes_daily_life: Reciting poems with correct rhythm helps a pupil perform confidently during school events such as poetry recitals or assemblies.
sla_exercise: Recite the first two lines of the poem.::'The sailor wants to sail. He sees a whale on the shore.'||What does the sailor see on the shore?::The sailor sees a whale on the shore.||Why can the sailor not sail at the end of the poem?::Because dense clouds, a big wave and rain come and put him in the shade, so there is no sailing.||Recite the poem's last line.::'There is no sailing!'

sla_name: Reading the passage about the hen's features fluently
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil reads the passage about the hen aloud fluently and answers simple comprehension questions about it.
sla_teaching_aids: Passage chart (Do you know what a hen is?)|Pupil's book Unit Eight
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Activity 4(c) presents a short informational passage about a hen and its beak, allowing pupils to practise fluent reading of connected sentences on a familiar topic.
sla_notes_details: The passage explains that a hen is a female chicken that lays eggs and describes how its sharp, strong beak helps it eat, drink, peck, crack seeds and nuts, and defend itself against predators such as foxes, hawks and snakes.
sla_notes_illustrations: From Activity 4(c): 'A hen is a female chicken that lays eggs.' 'It uses the beak to eat, drink and peck.' 'It can crack seeds, nuts and even small shells.' 'Examples of predators are foxes, hawks and snakes.'
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil who has read about the hen's beak can explain to family members why hens peck at grain in the compound at home.
sla_exercise: What is a hen?::A hen is a female chicken that lays eggs.||What does a hen use its beak for?::A hen uses its beak to eat, drink and peck, and to defend itself against predators.||Name two predators of the hen mentioned in the passage.::Foxes and hawks (or snakes).||What can the hen's beak crack?::The hen's beak can crack seeds, nuts and even small shells.

sla_name: Reading the story 'Maswi, the lucky boy' fluently with correct pronunciation
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil reads the story 'Maswi, the lucky boy' aloud fluently, correctly pronouncing short and long vowel words within it.
sla_teaching_aids: Story chart (Maswi, the lucky boy)|Pupil's book Unit Eight
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Activity 4(d) presents the story 'Maswi, the lucky boy,' a narrative that lets pupils practise reading longer connected text fluently while applying what they have learned about short and long vowel sounds.
sla_notes_details: The story tells how Maswi met five blind lions in a forbidden forest while walking, escaped by climbing a tree, waited until the lions left, and safely returned home to tell his parents, who said he was lucky.
sla_notes_illustrations: From Activity 4(d): 'A long time ago, there was a boy called Maswi. He lived with his parents in a remote village... Suddenly, he met five blind lions... He managed to climb up the tree... They all said that he was lucky.'
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil can retell the story of Maswi to younger siblings at home as a lesson about staying calm and thinking clearly in danger.
sla_exercise: Who is the main character in the story?::The main character is a boy called Maswi.||What did Maswi meet in the forbidden forest?::He met five blind lions.||How did Maswi escape from the lions?::He climbed up a tree and waited until the lions went into the wild.||What did Maswi's parents say when he told them what happened?::They said that he was lucky.

sla_name: Reading sentences with long vowel diphthong words (goat, boat, coat, bone, stove)
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil reads sentences containing diphthong-based long vowel words such as goat, boat, coat and stove clearly and correctly.
sla_teaching_aids: Sentence strips from Activity 4(e)|Word cards (goat, boat, coat, bone, stove)|Pupil's book Unit Eight
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Activity 4(e) presents sentences containing words with diphthong vowel sounds, giving pupils further practice reading words and sentences with long vowel-type sounds in context.
sla_notes_details: Pupils read sentences describing a goat and a foal in a boat, an owl caught with a bow and arrow, a coat and soap, a bowl full of meat, a toe cut with a hoe, a bone given to a dog, smoke from a burning house, and food cooked on a stove.
sla_notes_illustrations: From Activity 4(e): 'I saw a goat and a foal in a boat.' 'He bought a coat and a bar of soap.' 'He gave a bone to his dog.' 'We cook food on the stove.'
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil uses these words correctly when describing everyday activities at home, such as cooking food on a stove or giving a bone to a dog.
sla_exercise: Read aloud: 'I saw a goat and a foal in a boat.'::Pupil reads the sentence correctly, pronouncing goat, foal and boat clearly.||Read aloud: 'He gave a bone to his dog.'::Pupil reads the sentence correctly, pronouncing 'bone' clearly.||Read aloud: 'We cook food on the stove.'::Pupil reads the sentence correctly, pronouncing 'stove' clearly.||What did he cut his toe with?::He cut his toe with a hoe.

sla_name: Comprehension and retelling of 'Maswi, the lucky boy' using short and long vowel words
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil retells the story 'Maswi, the lucky boy' in their own words, correctly using words with short and long vowel sounds.
sla_teaching_aids: Story chart (Maswi, the lucky boy)|Sequence picture cards|Pupil's book Unit Eight
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD THREE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Beyond reading the story aloud, pupils build spoken fluency by retelling 'Maswi, the lucky boy' in their own words, applying correct pronunciation of short and long vowel words used in the story.
sla_notes_details: Pupils retell the sequence of events: Maswi walking in the forbidden forest, meeting five blind lions, climbing a tree to escape, waiting for the lions to leave, and returning home to his parents.
sla_notes_illustrations: From Activity 4(d): 'He shivered and bit his teeth in fear... He tried to climb the tree but failed. He tried again. He managed to climb up the tree.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Retelling stories aloud builds a pupil's confidence to narrate real events, such as describing what happened during a school trip.
sla_exercise: Where did Maswi live?::He lived with his parents in a remote village.||What was Maswi doing when he met the lions?::He was walking through the forbidden forest.||How did Maswi feel when the lions charged at him?::He shivered and bit his teeth in fear.||What lesson can we learn from the story?::Example: Stay calm and think clearly when facing danger.
